newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Grand British kitchens turn back the clock.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Grand British kitchens turn back the clock.

text.p: Britain is turning back the kitchen clock at its stately homes, resurrecting age-old recipes so today's visitors can taste the past.
From "likky pie" to "granny's leg", strange names and forgotten flavours are making a comeback at the National Trust, the world's biggest conservation charity.

"This is a plan to bring out the spirit of each house through food. These are homes rather than museums and the menus should reflect their history, surroundings and family anecdotes," said Jeremy Pearson, historic buildings representative at the Trust.

Food historians are already hard at work, poring over stained recipe books, yellowing diaries and county archives to discover the food fads of yesterday and transport visitors back in time via the stomach.
Trust chefs are even going back to school to learn the trade of their predecessors. The result tastes good -- even if some dishes sound unpromising.
Take "pug's choice": tender Cornish ham bathed in cider which is named after the top servants, called "pugs", by their inferiors in the hierarchical homes of yesteryear.
Or "granny's leg"5: a cylindrical, steamed orange pudding that was cooked in an old shirt sleeve and looks more like a lumpy old limb than desert.
Upside-down beetroot tart is a big hit, but visitors miss their chips when they eat Mediaeval, since food was routinely served on vast slabs of bread.
The potato had not yet reached the country.

"But to know someone enjoyed the very same dish in the very same house 100 years ago helps to reinforce the sense of living history. Our food was due for a re-vamp and this whole initiative is an attempt to make the past come alive," said Pearson.
EDIBLE HISTORY
The Trust, long accused of selling bland food in grand rooms, eventually wants to serve edible history at all its outlets, with 10 houses so far taking part.
At Lanhydrock, one of the most sumptuous houses in England's southwest, the old servants' quarters are once again thick with the floury smells of the last century.
Cooks were initially wary of stepping back -- "it was one big trauma, a nightmare at the start" said chef Alison Pearn -- but have since warmed to their new role.
The art of cooking from history requires no new culinary skills, she said, just investigative reporting and the ability to adapt and update where necessary.

Pearn trawled through an old Lanhydrock recipe book for a succulent mutton recipe with damson and plum sauce. The pungent mutton was swapped for lamb in squeamish Britain, but the sauce was authentic -- and popular.
A potato dish is topped with devilled mayonnaise, a spicy sauce that was all the rage under Queen Victoria when exotic imports grew along with the empire.

Far grander was the poached sea trout, which was offered to King George V1, Queen Elizabeth and Princess Margaret in 1950. It tastes delicate, fresh and modern: the queen declared it "the best meal she had ever eaten".

"When people talk about the history of British food, they think meat and two veg: really heavy, boring stuff," said Sara Paston-Williams, in charge of the historical menus initiative at the century-old Trust.
Everyday Victorian food, she admits, can be stodgy but Tudors had "fascinating" tastes and "Georgian is the epitome of English food taken to the height of elegance".
Yet Paston-Williams has bypassed the elaborate swan and offal feasts so beloved by the Victorians and the rank meat that often passed for food in Georgian days.
Tastes have changed; lifestyles have moved on.
"I am a purist but what I don't want to see is a fossilised version of historical dishes," she said.

So fruit cups and lemonades -- popular in Victorian days when women were not expected to drink -- sit alongside elegant New World wines, German beer and local scrumpy cider in an eclectic new-meets-old menus.
The result: new interest in the restaurant and more money for Lanhydrock, whose restaurant and shop make a combined 200,000 pounds ($324,000) a year.
"The figure is growing and the need for the money is growing too," said property manager Andrea Marchington.
"We have 49 rooms open here -- more than at any other Trust property -- and this sort of initiative really helps us pay for all that."
A stroll through the mellow Smoking Room or pannelled Billiard Room, both grand and empty, shows that crowds congregate thickest and longest in the kitchen.
From scullery to bakehouse to fish larder to dairy, the warren of rooms devoted to food goes on and on -- as do the crowds -- equipped with all mod cons of their day.

"Social history always appeals most," Marchington said. "It's the human details that really count, not the grand portraits, and after the visitors have found out whether his Lordship and her Ladyship shared a bath, they want to know exactly what went on in the kitchen." ($ = 0.615 British Pounds)
